----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the API documentation for the chameleon_rs library.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Templates

Compile and render templates from strings, files and folders.


PageTemplate(body: 'Any', **config: 'Any') -> 'None'

Constructor for the page template language, rendered by the Rust VM.

Takes a string input as the only positional argument::

  template = PageTemplate("<div>Hello, ${name}.</div>")

Output is of type ``str``. See the module docs for the configuration keywords.

Every template has the builtin ``render_partial(path, **kwargs)`` (D10, see
``chameleon_rs.partials``), which a render keyword or ``extra_builtins`` entry of the same
name overrides.

PageTemplateFile(filename: 'str | os.PathLike[str]', loader_class: 'type[TemplateLoader]' = <class 'chameleon_rs.loader.TemplateLoader'>, package_name: 'str | None' = None, search_path: 'Iterable[str | os.PathLike[str]] | str | os.PathLike[str] | None' = None, **config: 'Any') -> 'None'

File-based page template loaded from ``filename`` when first used.

With ``package_name``, ``filename`` is read from that package's resources.
File templates have the ``load:`` expression type, which loads templates relative to
this one: ``search_path`` (a path or a sequence of paths; with
``prepend_relative_search_path``, the default, the template's own directory comes first)
and ``loader_class`` (``TemplateLoader``), which gets the same configuration keywords.

PageTextTemplate(body: 'Any', **config: 'Any') -> 'None'

Text-based template class: only ``${...}`` interpolation, no markup, nothing escaped.

Takes a non-XML input::

  template = PageTextTemplate("Hello, ${name}.")

PageTextTemplateFile(filename: 'str | os.PathLike[str]', loader_class: 'type[TemplateLoader]' = <class 'chameleon_rs.loader.TemplateLoader'>, package_name: 'str | None' = None, search_path: 'Iterable[str | os.PathLike[str]] | str | os.PathLike[str] | None' = None, **config: 'Any') -> 'None'

File-based text template whose ``render()`` returns ``bytes`` (UTF-8 by default).

Encoded with the template's ``encoding`` (UTF-8 by default), as Chameleon's does.

TemplateLoader(search_path: 'Iterable[str | os.PathLike[str]] | str | os.PathLike[str] | None' = None, default_extension: 'str | None' = None, *, formats: 'Mapping[str, type[PageTemplateFile]] | None' = None, **kwargs: 'Any') -> 'None'

Loads and caches page templates from one or more directories by filename (``loader['page.pt']``).

Accepts a single directory path (``str`` or ``os.PathLike``) or an iterable of paths as
``search_path``, and passes extra keyword arguments (such as ``auto_reload`` or
``strict_tags``) to each template it constructs.


## PageTemplate Methods

Methods for the PageTemplate class


__getitem__(self, name: 'str') -> 'Macro'

engine

Chameleon's expression engine factory for this template's expression types.

Used by code that evaluates expressions dynamically, such as
``ExpressionEvaluator(template.engine, builtins)`` in z3c.pt for ``path()`` and
``exists()`` inside ``python:`` expressions. chameleon-rs compiles the template itself
natively and doesn't use it.

expression_parser

Chameleon's parser for this template's ``expression_types`` and ``default_expression``.

builtins

The template builtins: names every expression can use (overridden by render keywords).

parse(self, body: 'str') -> 'Any'

include

The whole template as a macro (``metal:use-macro="template"``).

Chameleon's ``include(stream, econtext, rcontext, ...)``, which renders the main
function into ``stream``.

render(self, encoding: 'str | None' = None, **kw: 'Any') -> 'str'

Render template to string.

If provided, the ``encoding`` argument overrides the template default value.
Additional keyword arguments are passed as template variables; ``translate``
overrides the template's translation function and ``target_language`` is the
language passed to it when no ``i18n:target`` applies.

render_async(self, encoding: 'str | None' = None, *, offload: 'bool' = False, **kw: 'Any') -> 'str'

Render template to string, awaiting awaitable values (D9).

The same as ``render``, except that when an expression's final value is awaitable (a
coroutine, a task, a future, anything ``await`` accepts), the render suspends until the
value is awaited and continues with its result. Values inside an expression are not
awaited (``coro().title`` is the coroutine's attribute), and a condition is tested on
the awaited value. An error raised by an awaited value is raised where the expression
is, so ``tal:on-error`` handles it; cancellation passes through.

Opt-in concurrency: calls of ``@chameleon_rs.concurrent`` helpers written as a whole
``${...}`` are awaited concurrently, and with the template setting ``concurrent=True``
native partials called with an awaitable argument render concurrently (see
``chameleon_rs._async``).

Experimental, opt-in: ``offload=True`` runs ``render`` (synchronous: awaitable values
are not awaited) in the event loop's default executor, a worker thread, and awaits it.
On a free-threaded build renders then run in parallel with the event loop and each
other; on a GIL build it helps only renders dominated by long text, whose escaping
releases the GIL (docs/plan.md, Phase 11 results). ``offload`` is therefore not a
template variable here.

digest(self, body: 'str', names: 'Collection[str]') -> 'str'


## Configuration

Process-wide settings for templates loaded by name, partials and Markdown.


configure(template_folder: 'str | os.PathLike[str] | None' = None, *, auto_reload: 'bool | None' = None, restricted_namespace: 'bool | None' = None, strict_tags: 'bool | None' = None, strict_names: 'bool | None' = None, partial_search: 'str | None' = None, markdown: 'MarkdownSetting | None' = None, markdown_cache: 'int | None' = None) -> 'Settings | None'

Configures chameleon-rs for the whole process (partials, framework integrations, and Markdown).

Sets where templates loaded by name live for ``render_partial`` and the framework
integrations (``chameleon_rs.flask``, ``chameleon_rs.starlette``,
``chameleon_rs.fastapi``, ``chameleon_rs.robyn``, ``chameleon_rs.litestar``), and how
they load.

``template_folder``: an existing directory. ``auto_reload``: recompile a template when its
file changes (checked at most once per file per render for partials). ``restricted_namespace``:
``False`` allows attributes such as Alpine.js's ``@click`` (chameleon-flask's option).
``strict_tags``: ``True`` makes an unclosed element carrying TAL, METAL or i18n attributes a
``ParseError`` at its start tag (default: ``CHAMELEON_STRICT_TAGS``, else off).
``strict_names``: ``True`` makes the integrations' decorator and module APIs (``@template``,
``render``, ``response``, ``ErrorPage.template_file``) refuse a template name that could
reach outside the template folder (absolute, ``..``, a backslash, a drive letter or package
spec, a NUL, surrounding whitespace) with the loader's ``ValueError('Template not found:
...')``, as for a missing file (default: ``CHAMELEON_STRICT_NAMES``, else off: they accept
such names, as the original libraries do).
``partial_search``: ``'caller'`` (the default: partials are looked for in the template
folder, then on the calling template's search path, then in its folder and each folder above
it, never outside its template tree) or ``'registered'`` (chameleon_partials' lookup: the template folder only, a path not
there being an error). ``markdown``: the ``markdown:`` expression types, ``True`` for
``markdown:`` with the defaults or a dict of profiles (prefix -> options, see the docs),
``False`` for none; it applies to templates compiled afterwards. ``markdown_cache``: how many
conversions to keep (``0``: no cache). A setting left out keeps its current value; the first
call that sets the folder's settings must give the folder (``partial_search`` and the
Markdown settings don't need one). Applies every time it is called (there is no
``cache_init``).

Raises ``chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError`` for a missing folder, ``ValueError`` for an
unknown ``partial_search`` or an invalid Markdown setting, ``TypeError`` for a Markdown
setting of the wrong type (nothing changes then).

core_version()

Version of the Rust core, for bug reports and for checking which build is loaded.


## Async

Opt-in concurrency for render_async. See also PageTemplate.render_async.


concurrent(fn: 'Callable[P, Awaitable[Any]]') -> 'Callable[P, ConcurrentCall]'

Marks an async helper so that an asynchronous render awaits its calls concurrently
(see the module docs).


## Partials

Render one template inside another. Also chameleon_partials' API.


render_partial(template_file: 'str', **template_data: 'Any') -> 'HTML'

Renders a partial template by path and returns an ``HTML`` object.

Used for ``chameleon_rs.render_partial`` (no calling template) and a template's own
``render_partial`` builtin (the calling template for ``partial_search='caller'``).
Written as a whole ``${render_partial(...)}`` expression it is not called at all: the
partial renders as a native frame.

register_extensions(template_folder: 'str', auto_reload: 'bool' = False, cache_init: 'bool' = True) -> 'None'

chameleon_partials' setup call: configures the folder ``render_partial`` uses (only
that; ``chameleon_rs.configure`` also configures the framework integrations). A second call
is ignored unless ``cache_init`` is false. Raises ``PartialsException`` for a missing
folder.

extend_model(model: 'dict[str, Any] | None') -> 'dict[str, Any]'

Adds ``render_partial`` to a view model (chameleon_partials' helper; not needed with the
built-in, which every template has). Returns the model (a new dict for ``None``).

clear() -> 'None'

Forgets the folder partials use, for tests.

function(template: 'Any' = None) -> 'None'

Renders a partial template by path and returns an ``HTML`` object.

Used for ``chameleon_rs.render_partial`` (no calling template) and a template's own
``render_partial`` builtin (the calling template for ``partial_search='caller'``).
Written as a whole ``${render_partial(...)}`` expression it is not called at all: the
partial renders as a native frame.

HTML(html_text: 'str') -> 'None'

Rendered markup, as ``render_partial`` returns it from Python: ``__html__`` gives the
text (``html_text``), so a template inserts it without escaping.

PartialsException

Raised when partials are configured or used incorrectly: registering a folder that does
not exist, or rendering a partial from Python before any folder is configured. Errors from
the templates themselves (``ValueError`` for a missing file) propagate unchanged.


## Flask and Quart

chameleon-flask's API, built in. Imports Flask only when imported itself.



## FastAPI

fastapi-chameleon's API, built in. Imports FastAPI only when imported itself.



## Starlette

Jinja2Templates' API for chameleon-rs, and the decorator API. Imports Starlette only when imported itself.



## Robyn

chameleon-robyn's API, built in. Imports Robyn only when imported itself.



## Litestar

Litestar's template engine interface for chameleon-rs, and the decorator API. Imports Litestar only when imported itself.



## Errors and web helpers

Exceptions, and the pieces shared by the framework integrations.


TemplateError(msg: 'str', token: 'str' = '') -> 'None'

Base class for compile-time template errors (``ParseError``, ``CompilationError``, ``ExpressionError``).

Carries the error message (``args[0]``) and the offending source ``token`` (``args[1]``),
with ``filename``, ``location`` (``(line, column)``), and ``offset`` properties.
Render-time exceptions are mixed with ``chameleon_rs.exc.RenderError`` instead.

TemplateError

A template integration was configured or used incorrectly: no template folder
configured, a folder that does not exist, a view returning something that is not a model
or a response. (Not a template compile error: that is ``chameleon_rs.TemplateError``.)

ErrorPage(template_file: 'str', status_code: 'int', message: 'str | None' = None, template_data: 'Mapping[str, Any] | None' = None) -> 'None'

Raised inside a decorated view to answer with an error page: the decorator renders
``template_file`` with ``template_data`` and ``status_code``.

NotFound(message: 'str | None' = None, template_file: 'str' = 'errors/404.pt', template_data: 'Mapping[str, Any] | None' = None) -> 'None'

Raised by ``not_found()``: the decorator renders ``template_file`` (``errors/404.pt``
by default) with status 404.

TemplateNotFound

No template of that name, or a name reaching outside the template folder: raised by
``chameleon_rs.starlette.Templates`` (the ``Jinja2Templates`` drop-in) and
``chameleon_rs.robyn.ChameleonTemplate`` (the ``JinjaTemplate`` drop-in), with the message
``Template not found: {name}.``; code moving from Jinja catches it where it caught
``jinja2.TemplateNotFound``. A ``ValueError`` (as Chameleon's loader raises) and a
``LookupError``. ``PageTemplateLoader`` and the other integrations raise Chameleon's plain
``ValueError``, unchanged.

DecoratorOrderError

A view was registered with its framework before ``@template`` wrapped it (``@template``
written above ``@app.get`` / ``@app.route`` / ``@router.get``), so the route calls the bare
view and the template never renders. Raised when the app starts (or on its first request),
for apps given to ``configure(app=...)`` or ``global_init(..., app=...)``, and by
``check_views(app)``.

model_of(value: 'Any') -> 'dict[str, Any] | None'

The template model a view returned: a ``dict`` as is; any other ``Mapping`` as a
``dict``; a dataclass instance as its fields (shallow: field values are not converted);
an object with a callable ``model_dump()`` (Pydantic, duck-typed) as what it returns.
``None`` for anything else.


## Compatibility

Make `import chameleon` resolve to chameleon-rs, or check both engines side by side.



----------------------------------------------------------------------
This is the User Guide documentation for the package.
----------------------------------------------------------------------


## Get started

### Getting started

This page installs chameleon-rs, renders a template from a string, then sets up a folder of
template files the way a web app would.

## Install

```bash
uv pip install chameleon-rs
```

chameleon-rs supports CPython 3.12 to 3.15, including the free-threaded builds (3.14t,
3.15t). The wheel contains the compiled engine and has no dependencies. The framework
integrations use the framework your app already has, so there are no extras to install.

## Render a template string

`PageTemplate` compiles a template from a string. Calling it renders the template, with the
keyword arguments as the template's variables:

```{python}
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate

page = PageTemplate("""
<div class="greeting">
  <h1>Hello, ${name}!</h1>
  <ul tal:condition="items">
    <li tal:repeat="item items">${repeat.item.number}. ${item}</li>
  </ul>
</div>
""")

print(page(name='World', items=['templates', 'in', 'Rust']))
```

The template compiles once, when it's first rendered. Every later render reuses the compiled
program, so keep template objects around (module level, or in a loader) rather than building
one per request.

`${...}` inserts a value with HTML escaping. To insert markup as-is, use `structure:`, or pass
an object with an `__html__` method:

```{python}
page = PageTemplate('<p>${text}</p> <p>${structure: text}</p>')
print(page(text='<b>bold</b>'))
```

## Render templates from files

`PageTemplateFile` loads one file. `PageTemplateLoader` loads templates by name from one or
more folders, and caches each compiled template:

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pathlib, tempfile

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'templates'
(folder / 'home').mkdir(parents=True)
(folder / 'shared').mkdir()
(folder / 'home' / 'index.pt').write_text(
    '<html>\n'
    '  <body>\n'
    '    <h1>${title}</h1>\n'
    '    <div tal:repeat="video videos">\n'
    "      ${render_partial('shared/video.pt', video=video)}\n"
    '    </div>\n'
    '  </body>\n'
    '</html>\n'
)
(folder / 'shared' / 'video.pt').write_text('<a href="/videos/${video.id}">${video.title}</a>')
template_folder = str(folder)
```

Suppose your templates live in a folder like this:

```text
templates/
├── home/
│   └── index.pt
└── shared/
    └── video.pt
```

with `home/index.pt`:

```html
<html>
  <body>
    <h1>${title}</h1>
    <div tal:repeat="video videos">
      ${render_partial('shared/video.pt', video=video)}
    </div>
  </body>
</html>
```

and `shared/video.pt`:

```html
<a href="/videos/${video.id}">${video.title}</a>
```

Configure the folder once at startup with `chameleon_rs.configure()`, then load templates by
name:

```{python}
from dataclasses import dataclass

import chameleon_rs
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplateLoader


@dataclass
class Video:
    id: int
    title: str


chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=template_folder)
templates = PageTemplateLoader([template_folder])

page = templates['home/index.pt']
print(page(title='Latest videos', videos=[Video(1, 'Intro'), Video(2, 'Partials')]))
```

`render_partial` is available in every template, with nothing to register or pass in.
`configure()` tells it where to find partials. See [Partials](partials.qmd).

In a real app, build the folder path relative to your code, so it doesn't depend on the
working directory:

```python
from pathlib import Path

import chameleon_rs

template_folder = Path(__file__).parent / 'templates'
chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)
```

`auto_reload=True` recompiles a template when its file changes. Turn it on in development and
leave it off in production.

## In a web app

In a web app you rarely call templates yourself. The framework integrations configure the
folder and render what your views return:

```python
import fastapi

import chameleon_rs.fastapi as fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode, app=app)


@app.get('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def index():
    return {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': await load_videos()}
```

[Web frameworks](frameworks.qmd) shows the same view in Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Starlette,
Robyn, Litestar and Pyramid, and links to each framework's guide.

## Next steps

- Already have a Chameleon app? See [Switching from Chameleon](switching-from-chameleon.qmd).
- Pick your framework: [Flask and Quart](flask.qmd), [FastAPI](fastapi.qmd),
  [Starlette](starlette.qmd), [Robyn](robyn.qmd), [Litestar](litestar.qmd) or
  [Pyramid](pyramid.qmd).
- Async views: [Async rendering](async.qmd) explains how a render awaits data without
  blocking the event loop.
- Content in Markdown? The [`markdown:` expression](markdown.qmd) converts it while the page
  renders.
- The [language reference](../language/index.qmd) covers TAL, METAL, i18n and expressions.


### Switching from Chameleon

chameleon-rs runs code written for Chameleon unchanged. There are two ways to switch: install
the compatibility alias and change nothing else, or change your imports.

## One line: `compat.install()`

Add this at the very top of your app's entry point (the module your server imports, or
`__main__`), before anything imports Chameleon:

```python
import chameleon_rs.compat

chameleon_rs.compat.install()
```

From then on:

| Your code imports | It gets |
|---|---|
| `chameleon`, `chameleon.zpt.template`, `chameleon.tales`, ... | the chameleon-rs module of the same name |
| `chameleon_partials` | `chameleon_rs.partials` (built in) |
| `chameleon_flask` (and `.engine`, `.exceptions`) | `chameleon_rs.flask` (built in) |
| `fastapi_chameleon` (and `.engine`, `.exceptions`) | `chameleon_rs.fastapi` (built in) |
| `chameleon_robyn` (and `.engine`, `.exceptions`) | `chameleon_rs.robyn` (built in) |

```{python}
import chameleon_rs.compat

chameleon_rs.compat.install()

import chameleon
from chameleon import PageTemplate

print(chameleon.__name__)
print(PageTemplate('<p>${1 + 1}</p>')())
```

Stock Chameleon doesn't need to be installed, and chameleon-rs never imports it. Libraries
that use Chameleon internally (litestar-chameleon, pyramid_chameleon, ...) get chameleon-rs the
same way. Their own test suites pass on it unmodified.

That includes libraries that subclass Chameleon's expression types, such as
[z3c.pt](https://pypi.org/project/z3c.pt/), the page template layer of Zope and Plone. Its
suite passes unmodified too. A template that names `PythonExpr` or another of Chameleon's types
directly gets the native compiler; a subclass compiles the way Chameleon compiles it, through
the bridge for [custom expression types](../language/expressions.qmd#custom-expression-types),
so its expressions run at the speed of an ordinary Python call. Each framework's guide is listed in
[Web frameworks](frameworks.qmd).

::: {.callout-warning}
## Install before the first import

`install()` must run before any module imports `chameleon`. If a module was already
imported, `install()` replaces it in `sys.modules` and warns with a `RuntimeWarning` that names
it. Objects imported from it earlier (`from chameleon import PageTemplateLoader` at the
top of a module that's already loaded) stay stock Chameleon objects.
:::

### Keep the original chameleon_partials or chameleon-flask

`install(integrations=False)` maps only `chameleon`. `chameleon_partials` and
`chameleon_flask` then import the original packages, which still render through
chameleon-rs's engine. Use it if you depend on behaviour of those packages that the built-ins
don't copy. A `chameleon_partials.render_partial` from the original package, passed into a
template, still renders natively.

## Or change the imports

Every public name is available from `chameleon_rs` directly:

```python
# Before
from chameleon import PageTemplate, PageTemplateFile, PageTemplateLoader
import chameleon_partials
import chameleon_flask

# After
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate, PageTemplateFile, PageTemplateLoader
import chameleon_rs.partials as chameleon_partials
import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask
```

The submodules mirror Chameleon's (`chameleon_rs.zpt.template`, `chameleon_rs.tales`,
`chameleon_rs.utils`, `chameleon_rs.exc`, ...). Chameleon's code-generation internals
(`chameleon.nodes`, `chameleon.program`, `chameleon.zpt.program`, `chameleon.benchmark`)
have no counterpart, since chameleon-rs doesn't generate Python code. Importing them raises
`ModuleNotFoundError`.

After switching, you can simplify: `render_partial` is in every template already, so
`extend_model()` calls and Pyramid `BeforeRender` subscribers that add it can go, and one
`chameleon_rs.configure()` call replaces `register_extensions()` plus `global_init()`. See
[Migrating from the helper libraries](migrating.qmd).

## Check your own app first: shadow mode

Before you switch a production app, you can run both engines side by side on real traffic.
Shadow mode keeps stock Chameleon serving and repeats a sample of renders with chameleon-rs,
then reports any difference in the output or in the exception raised:

```python
import chameleon_rs.shadow

chameleon_rs.shadow.install(sample_rate=0.05)   # serve Chameleon's output, check chameleon-rs's
# chameleon_rs.shadow.install(serve='rust')     # serve chameleon-rs's, check against Chameleon's
```

Differences are logged as warnings on the `chameleon_rs.shadow` logger, with a short diff.
Pass `report=` to handle each `ShadowDifference` yourself.

Shadow mode needs stock Chameleon installed, so don't combine it with `compat.install()`.
Keep in mind:

- Each sampled render happens twice, in the same thread, so its latency doubles. On a
  single-threaded asyncio server, both renders block the event loop. Keep `sample_rate` well
  below 1 (0.01 to 0.1).
- The model is used twice: an iterator argument is used up by the first render, and callables
  run twice. Shadow only side-effect-free renders.
- Templates compiled before `install()` aren't shadowed.

To stop, call `chameleon_rs.shadow.uninstall()`.



## Templates

### Template language

chameleon-rs implements Chameleon's template language unchanged: the same TAL attributes,
METAL macros, i18n attributes, `${...}` interpolation and expression types, with the same
output. Templates you wrote for Chameleon work as they are.

This page is a quick tour. The [language reference](../language/index.qmd) covers every
statement in detail.

## A tour in one template

```{python}
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate

page = PageTemplate("""
<section tal:define="count len(items)">
  <h2>${title} <small tal:condition="count">(${count})</small></h2>
  <p tal:condition="not count">Nothing here yet.</p>
  <ul>
    <li tal:repeat="item items"
        class="${'odd' if repeat.item.odd else 'even'}"
        tal:content="item.upper()">placeholder</li>
  </ul>
  <a href="${url}" tal:attributes="title url">More</a>
</section>
""")

print(page(title='Tags', items=['rust', 'python', 'html'], url='/tags'))
```

## The pieces

| Syntax | What it does |
|---|---|
| `${expr}` | Insert a value, HTML-escaped. Works in text and in attribute values. |
| `${structure: expr}` | Insert markup without escaping. Objects with `__html__` are also inserted as-is. |
| `tal:define="name expr"` | Bind a variable for the element and its children (`global` for the rest of the template). |
| `tal:condition="expr"` | Keep the element only if the expression is true. |
| `tal:repeat="item items"` | Repeat the element for each item. `repeat.item` gives `index`, `number`, `odd`, `even`, `start`, `end`, `length`, ... |
| `tal:content="expr"` / `tal:replace="expr"` | Replace the element's content, or the whole element. |
| `tal:attributes="name expr; ..."` | Set or remove attributes. |
| `tal:omit-tag=""` | Drop the element's tags and keep its content. |
| `tal:switch` / `tal:case` | Choose one of several branches. |
| `tal:on-error="expr"` | Render a fallback if the element raises. |
| `metal:define-macro` / `metal:use-macro` / `metal:fill-slot` | Layouts and reusable fragments. See below. |
| `i18n:translate`, `i18n:attributes`, `i18n:name`, `i18n:domain` | Mark text for translation. |

Expressions are Python by default. Other expression types are written with a prefix:
`string:`, `exists:`, `not:`, `import:`, `load:` and `structure:`.

## Layouts with METAL

A layout defines a macro with slots, and each page fills them:

```{python}
layout = PageTemplate("""
<html metal:define-macro="layout">
  <head><title metal:define-slot="title">Site</title></head>
  <body><main metal:define-slot="content"></main></body>
</html>
""")

page = PageTemplate("""
<html metal:use-macro="layout.macros['layout']">
  <title metal:fill-slot="title">Home</title>
  <main metal:fill-slot="content"><p>Welcome, ${user}.</p></main>
</html>
""")

print(page(layout=layout, user='Ada'))
```

In a template loaded from a file, `load:` loads the layout relative to the page:
`metal:use-macro="load: ../shared/_layout.pt"`.

## What chameleon-rs adds

Two additions, both of which leave existing templates unchanged:

- **`render_partial`**, a builtin in every template:
  `${render_partial('shared/card.pt', item=item)}`. See [Partials](partials.qmd).
- **`markdown:`**, an expression type you turn on with
  `chameleon_rs.configure(markdown=True)`: `${markdown: post.body}`. See
  [Markdown](markdown.qmd).

And one way to render: `await template.render_async(**model)` awaits awaitable values where
the template uses them. The language is the same; see [Async rendering](async.qmd).


### Partials

A partial is a template file rendered inside another template, with its own small model. Use
them for anything you repeat: a card in a listing, a form field, a table row, a fragment you
also return on its own to HTMX (see [HTMX](htmx.qmd)).

chameleon-rs has partials built in. Every template can call `render_partial`, with nothing
to register or pass in:

```html
<div tal:repeat="video videos">
  ${render_partial('shared/partials/video_card.pt', video=video, show_date=True)}
</div>
```

`render_partial(path, **kwargs)` renders the template at `path` with `kwargs` as its
variables, and inserts the result unescaped. Written as a whole `${...}` expression, as above,
it doesn't make a Python call at all: the partial renders as a native frame of the page. That
makes a listing of partials about 10x faster than Chameleon with chameleon_partials.

## Tell chameleon-rs where templates live

```python
import chameleon_rs

chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=template_folder)
```

Call it once at startup. See [Configuration](configuration.qmd) for its other options.

## How a path is found

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pathlib, tempfile

root = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'templates'
for sub in ('shared', 'admin/users'):
    (root / sub).mkdir(parents=True)
(root / 'shared' / 'badge.pt').write_text('<span class="badge">${label}</span>')
(root / 'admin' / 'users' / 'row.pt').write_text('<tr><td>${user}</td><td>${render_partial("shared/badge.pt", label="admin")}</td></tr>')
(root / 'admin' / 'users' / 'list.pt').write_text(
    '<table>\n'
    '  <tal:row repeat="user users">${render_partial(\'row.pt\', user=user)}</tal:row>\n'
    '</table>\n'
)
template_folder = str(root)
```

By default, `render_partial` looks for the path in these places, in order:

1. The configured template folder.
2. The calling template's search path: the folders of the `PageTemplateLoader` that loaded
   it.
3. The calling template's own folder, then each folder above it, up to the root of its
   template tree.

The root is the configured template folder (for partials or for a framework integration,
whatever the folder is named) or the loader search path entry that holds the calling
template. With nothing configured, it is the nearest folder named `templates` whose parent is
a Python package, as in a Pyramid app (`myapp/templates/`, next to `myapp/__init__.py`). With
none of these, only the template's own folder is searched.

The search never leaves that tree: a path that would end up outside it, through `..` or
because it is absolute, is not found there. The configured folder is held to the same rule,
and a `package:path` spec is refused there too, as chameleon_partials does from 0.2.1. That way a file outside your templates, such as
one in a parent folder or a system file, is never compiled as a template.

If the path isn't found anywhere, the render raises `ValueError('Template not found: <path>.')`.

So a page can use partials that sit next to it, with a short path:

```text
templates/
├── shared/
│   └── badge.pt
└── admin/users/
    ├── list.pt      ${render_partial('row.pt', user=user)}
    └── row.pt       ${render_partial('shared/badge.pt', label='admin')}
```

```{python}
import chameleon_rs
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplateLoader

chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=template_folder)
templates = PageTemplateLoader([template_folder])

print(templates['admin/users/list.pt'](users=['ada', 'grace']))
```

`row.pt` isn't in the template folder's root, so it's found next to `list.pt`.
`shared/badge.pt` is found in the template folder.

Each resolution is cached until the configuration changes, so the search happens once per
path and calling template.

### chameleon_partials' lookup: `partial_search='registered'`

chameleon_partials resolves every path against the registered folder only, and treats any
other path as an error. To get exactly that behaviour:

```python
chameleon_rs.configure(partial_search='registered')
```

The default only differs from chameleon_partials where chameleon_partials would raise, so
templates that work there work the same way here.

## What a partial sees

A partial sees only the keyword arguments you pass it, plus `render_partial` itself. It
doesn't see the calling template's variables. Pass what it needs explicitly:

```html
${render_partial('shared/user_card.pt', user=user, is_admin=is_admin)}
```

## Calling it from Python

`chameleon_rs.render_partial` renders a partial from Python code: in a view that returns an
HTMX fragment, in an email builder, or in a test. It returns an `HTML` object. Its
`html_text` attribute is the markup, and its `__html__` method means a template inserts it
without escaping:

```{python}
fragment = chameleon_rs.render_partial('shared/badge.pt', label='new')
print(type(fragment).__name__, repr(fragment.html_text))
```

From Python there's no calling template, so the path is looked up in the configured folder
only. If no folder is configured, it raises `chameleon_rs.partials.PartialsException`.

## chameleon_partials' API

`chameleon_rs.partials` is also chameleon_partials' API, so code written for it keeps
working. With `chameleon_rs.compat.install()`, `import chameleon_partials` gives this module.

| chameleon_partials | chameleon-rs |
|---|---|
| `register_extensions(folder, auto_reload=False, cache_init=True)` | Still works. Configures partials only. `chameleon_rs.configure()` configures partials and the framework integrations. |
| `render_partial(path, **model)` | Same, and also a builtin in every template. |
| `extend_model(model)` | Still works, but isn't needed: every template already has `render_partial`. |
| `PartialsException` | Same. Also a subclass of `chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError`. |
| `HTML` | Same (`html_text`, `__html__`). |
| `has_registered_extensions = False` (test reset) | Still works. `chameleon_rs.partials.clear()` is the direct call. |

::: {.callout-note}
## Reserved names

As in chameleon_partials, a partial renders as if called with `encoding='utf-8'`, so don't
use `encoding` as a model name. `translate`, `target_language` and `repeat` also have special
meanings in any Chameleon template.
:::


### HTMX

[HTMX](https://htmx.org) swaps part of a page with an HTML fragment the server returns.
chameleon-rs has what that needs built in. [Partials](partials.qmd) (chameleon_partials, built
in) are the fragments, and every framework integration can return one on its own. There is
nothing extra to install or register.

The pattern is the one chameleon_partials was written for. Put the piece of the page HTMX
replaces in its own template. The full page includes it with `render_partial`, and the view
HTMX calls renders only that template. Because both use the same file, the first page load and
the HTMX response can't drift apart.

## One template, two uses

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pathlib, tempfile, warnings

# Starlette's TestClient warns about httpx on import; not part of the example.
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', message='Using `httpx`')

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'templates'
(folder / 'search').mkdir(parents=True)
(folder / 'search' / 'results.pt').write_text(
    '<ul id="results">\n'
    '  <li tal:repeat="episode results">${episode}</li>\n'
    '</ul>'
)
(folder / 'search' / 'index.pt').write_text(
    '<input type="search" name="q" value="${q}"\n'
    '       hx-get="/search" hx-trigger="input changed delay:300ms"\n'
    '       hx-target="#results" hx-swap="outerHTML" hx-push-url="true">\n'
    "${render_partial('search/results.pt', results=results)}"
)
template_folder = str(folder)
```

A search box that updates the results as you type. The fragment, `search/results.pt`:

```html
<ul id="results">
  <li tal:repeat="episode results">${episode}</li>
</ul>
```

The page, `search/index.pt`, includes it:

```html
<input type="search" name="q" value="${q}"
       hx-get="/search" hx-trigger="input changed delay:300ms"
       hx-target="#results" hx-swap="outerHTML" hx-push-url="true">
${render_partial('search/results.pt', results=results)}
```

The partial renders as a native frame of the page (see [Partials](partials.qmd)), so including
it costs about the same as writing its markup inline.

## Full page or fragment from one view

HTMX sends an `HX-Request: true` header with every request it makes. One view can check it,
returning the fragment to HTMX and the whole page to everyone else: a first visit, a reload,
or a shared link to a URL that `hx-push-url` put in the address bar. With FastAPI:

```{python}
import fastapi

import chameleon_rs.fastapi as fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.configure(template_folder=template_folder, app=app)

EPISODES = ['Python 3.14', 'Rust for Pythonistas', 'HTMX in practice']


async def find(q: str) -> list[str]:
    return [e for e in EPISODES if q.lower() in e.lower()]


def wants_fragment(request: fastapi.Request) -> bool:
    headers = request.headers
    return 'HX-Request' in headers and 'HX-History-Restore-Request' not in headers


@app.get('/search')
async def search(request: fastapi.Request, q: str = ''):
    results = await find(q)
    if wants_fragment(request):
        return await fastapi_chameleon.response_async('search/results.pt', results=results)
    return await fastapi_chameleon.response_async('search/index.pt', q=q, results=results)
```

```{python}
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

client = TestClient(app)
print(client.get('/search', params={'q': 'py'}, headers={'HX-Request': 'true'}).text)
```

When the back button finds a page missing from its history cache, HTMX fetches it again with
`HX-History-Restore-Request: true` as well and expects the whole page, which is why
`wants_fragment` checks for that header too. If a cache sits in front of the app, send
`Vary: HX-Request` so it doesn't serve one response in place of the other.

Every integration has the same `response()` and `response_async()`: `chameleon_rs.flask`,
`chameleon_rs.starlette`, `chameleon_rs.robyn` and `chameleon_rs.litestar` as well as
`chameleon_rs.fastapi`.

## A view that only returns the fragment

When a route exists only for HTMX, such as an `hx-post` that adds a row, put `@template` on
the fragment itself:

```python
@app.post('/todos')                          # the route decorator first...
@fastapi_chameleon.template('todos/list.pt') # ...then @template, naming the fragment
async def add(title: str = fastapi.Form()):
    await db.add_todo(title)
    return {'todos': await db.todos()}
```

A partial is an ordinary template, so the decorators render it like any page, async views
included: an `async def` view renders with `render_async` and doesn't block the event loop
(see [Async rendering](async.qmd)).

## From Python, without a framework

`chameleon_rs.render_partial(path, **model)` renders a fragment anywhere: an HTMX view in a
framework without an integration, a WebSocket or server-sent events handler pushing HTML, or a
test. It returns an `HTML` object whose `html_text` is the markup:

```{python}
import chameleon_rs

fragment = chameleon_rs.render_partial('search/results.pt', results=['HTMX in practice'])
print(fragment.html_text)
```

From Python the path is looked up in the configured template folder only, as with
chameleon_partials. The [HTMX fragments](../recipes/htmx-fragments.qmd) recipe shows the same
idea with Flask.


### Markdown

chameleon-rs can convert Markdown to HTML while it renders, with a `markdown:` expression:

```html
<article>${markdown: episode.notes}</article>
<div tal:content="markdown: comment.text"></div>
```

It's opt-in: Chameleon has nothing like it, so you turn it on with `configure()` and use it in
new templates. The converter is built into chameleon-rs (comrak, in Rust), so there's no
Markdown package to install.

## Turn it on

```{python}
import chameleon_rs
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate

chameleon_rs.configure(markdown=True)

page = PageTemplate('<article>${markdown: notes}</article>')
print(page(notes='# Show notes\n\nWe talked about **templates** and `Rust`.'))
```

`configure(markdown=True)` registers the `markdown:` prefix with the defaults. Call it once at
startup, before your templates compile: a template takes the Markdown settings in effect when
it's compiled.

## What it supports

[CommonMark](https://commonmark.org/) plus the GitHub extensions: tables, strikethrough, task
lists, autolinks for bare URLs, and footnotes.

```{python}
notes = """\
| Engine | Speed |
|---|---|
| chameleon-rs | ~~slow~~ fast |

- [x] Ship it, see https://example.com
"""
print(page(notes=notes))
```

Fenced code blocks get a `language-…` class, so a client-side highlighter such as highlight.js
or Prism can color them:

```{python}
print(page(notes='```python\nprint("hi")\n```'))
```

## Values

- The text after `markdown:` is an ordinary expression, so a `|` fallback works:
  `markdown: episode.notes | 'No notes yet.'`. As everywhere in TALES, the fallback is used when
  the expression raises (a missing attribute, say), not when its value is `None`.
- `None` and `''` render nothing. Any other non-string value is converted with `str()` first.
- `default` works as for any expression: `tal:content="markdown: page.notes | default"` keeps
  the element's own content when `page.notes` is missing.
- The result is markup, like `structure:`, so it isn't escaped again in element content.
- In an attribute value (`alt="${markdown: x}"`, `tal:attributes`), the result is escaped like
  any string. Markdown's HTML has quoted attributes of its own (`<a href="...">`), which would
  otherwise close the surrounding attribute and let the text add new ones, such as an event
  handler. Use Markdown in element content; `${structure: markdown: x}` writes it raw anyway.

```{python}
print(PageTemplate('<div>${markdown: missing.notes | "*Coming soon*"}</div>')())
print(PageTemplate('<p>[${markdown: notes}]</p>')(notes=None))
```

## Safe by default

Raw HTML in the Markdown is shown as text, not passed through. That's the right default for
text you don't fully control, such as user comments:

```{python}
print(page(notes='Nice post! <script>alert("hi")</script>'))
```

Links with a `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, `file:` or `data:` URL (other than an image) lose the URL too.

For content you trust, such as your own articles, allow raw HTML in a separate profile (see
below). `raw_html: 'allow'` lets those URLs through as well.

"Safe" here is about markup and requests, not CPU time. Some inputs are slow to convert: a
table with thousands of columns can take seconds. If anyone can post the text, limit its
length when you accept it, and consider turning tables off for that profile
(`'extensions': {'table': False}`).

Tables have a memory budget. Every row of a table gets as many cells as its header, so a
short text can ask for millions of empty ones (a header of 700 columns over 700 one-cell
rows, a few times over). Text whose tables would make more than 100,000 cells, or more cells
than it has bytes, converts with tables off: their rows show as plain paragraphs.

## Profiles: one prefix per kind of content

Different content needs different settings: your own articles may allow HTML, while comments
shouldn't even load images. Each profile is its own expression prefix:

```{python}
chameleon_rs.configure(markdown={
    'markdown': {},                                     # the defaults
    'md-trusted': {'raw_html': 'allow', 'heading_ids': True},
    'md-comment': {'images': False},
    'md-inline': {'inline': True},
})

page = PageTemplate("""\
<h1>${md-inline: post.title}</h1>
<article>${md-trusted: post.body}</article>
<div tal:repeat="c post.comments">${md-comment: c}</div>
""")


class Post:
    title = 'Hello *world*'
    body = '## Intro\n\nSome <abbr title="HyperText Markup Language">HTML</abbr>.'
    comments = ['Look: ![tracker](https://example.com/pixel.png)']


print(page(post=Post()))
```

A profile name is a prefix, so it uses lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`, and can't be
one of Chameleon's own (`python`, `string`, `structure`, ...). A template class that defines a
prefix itself in `expression_types` keeps its own.

### Profile options

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `raw_html` | `'escape'` | `'escape'` shows raw HTML as text. `'allow'` passes it through: trusted content only. |
| `images` | `True` | `False` renders an image as its alt text, so the text can't make the page load a remote image. |
| `inline` | `False` | Drops the `<p>` around output that's a single paragraph, for titles and one-liners in element content (`<h1>${md-inline: title}</h1>`). |
| `heading_ids` | `False` | `True` gives headings GitHub-style ids and anchor links. A string adds a prefix to each id, such as `'doc-'` (letters, digits, `-` and `_`). |
| `classes` | `{}` | A class attribute per element, such as `{'table': 'table is-striped', 'pre': 'code'}`. Elements: `p`, `h1`–`h6`, `blockquote`, `ul`, `ol`, `li`, `pre`, `code`, `table`, `a`, `img`, `hr`. See the notes below. |
| `extensions` | all on | Switch GFM extensions off: `{'table': False}`. Keys: `table`, `strikethrough`, `tasklist`, `autolink`, `footnotes`. |

```{python}
chameleon_rs.configure(markdown={'markdown': {'classes': {'table': 'table is-striped', 'blockquote': 'note'}}})
print(PageTemplate('${markdown: s}')(s='> Tip\n\n| a |\n|---|\n| 1 |'))
```

Notes on `classes`:

- Only elements the Markdown produces get a class. Raw HTML in the text never does.
- `code` is inline code. A fenced block's `<code>` keeps its `language-…` class; style it
  through `pre`.
- The footnote list, footnote references and back-links, and heading anchor links don't get
  the `ol`, `li` and `a` classes. Footnote paragraphs do get the `p` class.
- A paragraph inside a tight list (no blank lines between items) has no `<p>` tag, so it gets
  no `p` class.

Each conversion numbers its heading ids on its own, so two `markdown:` blocks with
`heading_ids` on one page can repeat an id. Give each block a profile with its own prefix.

For text from users, always give `heading_ids` a prefix (`'user-content-'`, as GitHub does).
Without one, a heading such as `# csrf_token` gets `id="csrf_token"`, and an element id can
shadow a JavaScript global of the same name or answer `getElementById` before your own
element does.

A bad setting raises `ValueError` (or `TypeError` for a value of the wrong type) when you call
`configure()`, and changes nothing.

## Speed and the cache

The converter is fast: a 5 KB document with tables, lists, code and footnotes converts in
about 55 µs, about 26x faster than mistune with the same extensions.

On top of that, chameleon-rs keeps recent conversions in a cache shared by all threads: the
same text with the same profile isn't converted twice. A cache hit costs about 0.3 µs for a
5 KB document. The cache holds 1,024 conversions by default, and at most 64 MB of text and
HTML whatever the count. Texts over 64 KB are converted every time rather than cached:

```python
chameleon_rs.configure(markdown_cache=4096)   # entries; 0 turns the cache off
```

Changing the Markdown settings empties the cache.

## Async renders

`render_async` works with `markdown:`. If the value is awaitable (`${markdown: load_body()}`
with an `async def load_body()`), it is awaited and then converted, and a `@concurrent` helper
still runs alongside the page's other concurrent calls. As for every expression type, only the
expression's value is awaited, not values inside it: `${markdown: body().text}` reads `.text`
of the coroutine. A synchronous `render` converts what it gets, so load the text in your view
there.


### Async rendering

Chameleon renders synchronously. In an async web app (FastAPI, Starlette, Quart, Litestar,
Robyn) that means a render runs on the event loop, and nothing else in that worker runs until
it finishes. chameleon-rs keeps `render()` exactly as it was and adds `render_async()`, which
renders on the event loop without holding it while it waits for data.

The framework integrations use it for you: an `async def` view decorated with `@template`
renders with `render_async`. This page explains what that does, and the opt-in extras built on
it.

## `render_async`

`await template.render_async(**model)` renders like `render()`, except that when a value the
template uses is awaitable (a coroutine, task or future), the render awaits it right there
and continues with the result. While it waits, the event loop serves other requests.

```{python}
import asyncio

from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate

page = PageTemplate("""\
<h1>${title}</h1>
<ul>
  <li tal:repeat="episode episodes">${episode}</li>
</ul>
""")


async def latest_episodes():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.01)   # a database query, say
    return ['Rust for Python devs', 'Async templates']


print(await page.render_async(title='Latest', episodes=latest_episodes()))
```

`latest_episodes()` is passed unawaited. The render reaches `tal:repeat`, awaits it, and
repeats over the list it returns.

With no awaitable values, `render_async()` gives exactly `render()`'s output. That's tested
against every Chameleon fixture template and the render fuzzers, so switching a view from
`render()` to `render_async()` changes nothing until you pass it something to await.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Loading data in the view is still a good default

You don't have to hand coroutines to the template. Loading the data in the view (or a view
model) with `asyncio.gather` keeps data access in one place and makes the template a pure
function of its model:

```python
async def episode_page(number: int):
    episode, related = await asyncio.gather(db.episode(number), db.related(number))
    return {'episode': episode, 'related': related}
```

`render_async` still matters then: the integrations need no change in your views, and a big
page can render in a thread (see [Offloading](#offloading-a-render-to-a-thread)). Without
that, the render itself runs on the loop: an async render yields only where a value
suspends, so a page that is all CPU work (a 500,000-row table) holds the loop until it is
done, as a synchronous render would. Passing awaitables to the template is useful when a value is only sometimes used (a
sidebar behind a `tal:condition`), so it is never loaded when the page doesn't show it.
:::

## What gets awaited

Only an expression's **final value** is awaited:

| Template | With `episodes=load()` (a coroutine) |
|---|---|
| `${episodes}`, `tal:content="episodes"` | Awaited, then inserted. |
| `tal:repeat="e episodes"` | Awaited, then repeated over. |
| `tal:condition="episodes"` | Awaited, and the condition tested on the result. |
| `tal:define="items episodes"` | Awaited once; `items` is the result. |
| `${episodes.count}` | Not awaited: `.count` is looked up on the coroutine, an `AttributeError` as in a sync render. |
| `${len(episodes)}` | Not awaited: `len()` gets the coroutine. |

So pass the awaitable the template needs as a whole, or `tal:define` it first and use the
result:

```{python}
page = PageTemplate("""\
<p tal:define="items episodes">${len(items)} episodes, the first is ${items[0]}.</p>
""")
print(await page.render_async(episodes=latest_episodes()))
```

Async iterables (an `async def` generator) aren't supported in `tal:repeat`, as they aren't
iterable in a sync render either. Collect them in a helper first:
`[x async for x in source]`.

## Errors, macros and partials

Everything in the language works across a wait:

- **Macros and slots.** A layout's macro and the page's slot fills can await values.
- **Partials.** `${render_partial('shared/card.pt', item=item)}` renders natively, and the
  partial can await values of its own.
- **`tal:on-error`.** An exception raised by an awaited value is raised where the expression
  is, so the nearest `tal:on-error` handles it, as for any other error.
- **Cancellation.** Cancelling the task that runs the render cancels the value being awaited.

```{python}
async def broken():
    raise LookupError('the recommendations service is down')


page = PageTemplate("""\
<aside tal:on-error="string:Recommendations are unavailable.">
  <p tal:repeat="r recommendations">${r}</p>
</aside>
""")
print(await page.render_async(recommendations=broken()))
```

## Running helpers concurrently

By default the render awaits one value at a time, in document order. A page that calls three
slow helpers waits for each in turn. Two opt-in settings let them run at the same time. Both
change the order in which your code runs, which is why they're off by default.

### `@chameleon_rs.concurrent` helpers

Decorate an async helper with `@chameleon_rs.concurrent`, and each call to it written as a
whole `${...}` starts as a task. The render writes a placeholder and keeps going, and each
placeholder is filled in, escaped as usual, when the render reaches the end:

```{python}
import time

import chameleon_rs


@chameleon_rs.concurrent
async def fetch(name, delay):
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    return f'{name} ({delay}s)'


page = PageTemplate("""\
<p>${fetch('downloads', 0.2)}</p>
<p>${fetch('reviews', 0.2)}</p>
<p>${fetch('sponsors', 0.2)}</p>
""")

start = time.perf_counter()
print(await page.render_async(fetch=fetch))
print(f'{time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s, not 0.6s')
```

A call runs concurrently only where its output can simply be written later: a whole `${...}`
in text, or one inside an attribute value. Anywhere its value decides what the template does
(a condition, a `tal:define`, `tal:content` / `tal:replace`, which may choose the default
content) or where the output might be taken back (inside `tal:on-error` or a translation), it is
awaited in place, like any awaitable.

If a concurrent call raises, the render waits for nothing else: the error is raised as soon as
the render has reached its end and that call has failed, even if calls before it in the page are
still running. The other tasks are cancelled and their `finally` blocks run before the error is
raised, as in a `TaskGroup`. If the request is cancelled meanwhile, the `CancelledError` (or
`asyncio.timeout`'s `TimeoutError`) wins over the template error. In a sync `render()` the
decorator has no effect.

One render starts at most 64 tasks for concurrent calls and partials (set
`CHAMELEON_CONCURRENT_LIMIT` to change it). Past that, each further call is awaited where it
stands, so a `tal:repeat` over request-sized data can't start an unbounded number of queries at
once.

### Partials in parallel: `concurrent=True`

A template created with `concurrent=True` also renders its `render_partial(...)` calls
concurrently, when a call has an awaitable argument. Each such partial renders as a render of
its own, in a task:

```{python}
import pathlib, tempfile

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
(folder / 'card.pt').write_text('<div class="card">${data}</div>')
chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=str(folder))


async def load(name):
    await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
    return name


page = PageTemplate("""\
<section tal:repeat="name names">${render_partial('card.pt', data=load(name))}</section>
""", concurrent=True)

start = time.perf_counter()
print(await page.render_async(names=['a', 'b', 'c'], load=load))
print(f'{time.perf_counter() - start:.1f}s')
```

The integrations take the same setting on the decorator: `@template('page.pt',
concurrent=True)`, and `TemplateResponse_async(..., concurrent=True)` for Starlette's
`Templates`.

## Offloading a render to a thread

Experimental. `render_async(..., offload=True)` (or `@template(..., offload=True)`) runs the
render in a worker thread (the event loop's default executor) and awaits it. The render is
synchronous there, so awaitable values aren't awaited: load the data first.

- **On free-threaded Python (3.14t, 3.15t)** renders then run in parallel with the event loop
  and with each other. chameleon-rs ships free-threaded wheels and doesn't turn the GIL back
  on.
- **On a regular (GIL) build** it helps only pages dominated by long text, whose escaping
  releases the GIL. For most pages, a thread hop costs more than it saves.
- **Cancellation**: a render still waiting for a thread is dropped when its request is cancelled
  (a client disconnect), but one already running in a thread can't be interrupted: it finishes
  and its result is discarded.

## In the web frameworks

Every integration renders `async def` views with `render_async`, so all of the above applies
to the model a view returns:

| Integration | `async def` view | Plain `def` view |
|---|---|---|
| [Flask and Quart](flask.qmd) | `render_async` (Flask's async views, Quart) | `render()` |
| [FastAPI](fastapi.qmd) | `render_async` on the event loop | `render()` in FastAPI's thread pool |
| [Starlette](starlette.qmd) | `render_async`, and `await templates.TemplateResponse_async(...)` | `render()` in Starlette's thread pool |
| [Robyn](robyn.qmd) | `render_async` on Robyn's event loop | `render()` on Robyn's worker thread |
| [Litestar](litestar.qmd) | `render_async` with `@template`; `ChameleonEngine` (Litestar's `Template` responses) always renders synchronously | `render()`, in a thread with `sync_to_thread=True` |

Each module also has `render_async()` and `response_async()`, the coroutine versions of
`render()` and `response()`.

::: {.callout-note}
## A difference from the original libraries

chameleon-flask, fastapi-chameleon and chameleon-robyn rendered async views synchronously, so
an awaitable in the model was inserted as the object itself (`<coroutine object ...>`). The
built-ins await it. That includes test doubles such as `AsyncMock()` in a model.
:::

## Things to know

- **`markdown:` and other expression types** follow the same rule: the expression's final
  value is awaited. Load Markdown text before rendering rather than passing a coroutine for
  `markdown:` to convert.
- **A subclass that overrides `render()`** keeps its override: `render_async()` calls it,
  synchronously, so awaitable values aren't awaited. A monkeypatched `PageTemplate.render`
  (to time renders, say) counts as an override. See
  [Migrating](migrating.qmd#timing-renders).
- **`render()` never awaits.** In a sync render a coroutine in the model is just an object,
  as in Chameleon.


### Catching unclosed tags

A common complaint about Chameleon is that a template mistake gets reported far from where
it is. The usual cause is an unclosed tag, and chameleon-rs can catch it where it happens
with one setting: `strict_tags`.

## The problem

When Chameleon finds a start tag with no matching end tag, it treats the tag as an empty
element and carries on. Any `tal:`, `metal:` or `i18n:` attribute on that tag then applies to
the tag alone, not to the content you meant it to cover. The template compiles without
complaint, and one of two things happens.

**It renders the wrong thing, with no error.** Here the missing `</div>` means
`tal:condition` hides an empty `<div>`, and the "secret" paragraph shows anyway:

```{python}
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplate

page = PageTemplate("""
<section>
  <div tal:condition="user.is_admin">
    <p>Admin tools</p>
</section>
""")

class User:
    is_admin = False

print(page(user=User()))
```

**Or it fails somewhere else.** Here the missing `</ul>` is on line 3, but the error names a
variable on line 4. In a real page the symptom can be dozens of lines from the cause.

```{python}
page = PageTemplate("""
<main>
  <ul tal:repeat="episode episodes">
    <li>${episode}</li>
</main>
""")

try:
    page(episodes=['Rust', 'Python'])
except NameError as e:
    print('NameError:', '\n'.join(str(e).splitlines()[:4]))
```

## The fix: `strict_tags`

With `strict_tags=True`, the unclosed tag is a `ParseError` when the template compiles. The
error points at the tag that's missing its end tag, and says what to add:

```{python}
from chameleon_rs.exc import ParseError

source = """
<main>
  <ul tal:repeat="episode episodes">
    <li>${episode}</li>
</main>
"""

try:
    PageTemplate(source, strict_tags=True)
except ParseError as e:
    print(e)
```

## Turning it on

It's off by default, because Chameleon accepts these templates and chameleon-rs matches
Chameleon unless you ask otherwise. Turn it on in whichever way suits you:

- **For the whole process:** `chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder='templates', strict_tags=True)`.
  That covers `render_partial` and every framework integration, including the frameworks'
  own `configure()` calls made afterwards.
- **Without changing code:** set the environment variable `CHAMELEON_STRICT_TAGS=1`. This is
  handy in development and in tests. Together with `CHAMELEON_EAGER=1`, a test that loads
  every template catches these mistakes before they ship.
- **Per template or loader:** `PageTemplate(source, strict_tags=True)`,
  `PageTemplateFile(path, strict_tags=True)` or `PageTemplateLoader(folder, strict_tags=True)`.

It's also safe to leave on in production. It only adds a check at compile time, so rendering
speed doesn't change. All 229 templates of two production sites compile with it on.

## What it checks

An element is reported when it has no end tag, isn't self-closed with `/>`, and either:

- carries a `tal:`, `metal:` or `i18n:` attribute (or a `data-tal-*` one with
  `enable_data_attributes`), or
- is itself in one of those namespaces, such as `<tal:block>`.

These are still allowed:

- HTML's void elements, which never have an end tag: `<input tal:attributes="...">`,
  `<img>`, `<br>`, `<meta>`, `<link>` and the rest.
- Unclosed elements without template attributes, such as HTML's optional `</p>` and `</li>`.
  They render the same either way.
- `${...}` in an unclosed element's attributes. An interpolation affects only its own
  attribute, so nothing is lost.


### Configuration

chameleon-rs has three layers of configuration:

1. **`chameleon_rs.configure()`**: process-wide settings for templates loaded by name, used by
   `render_partial` and the framework integrations.
2. **Template options**: keyword arguments to the template classes and `PageTemplateLoader`,
   exactly as in Chameleon.
3. **Environment variables**: Chameleon's `CHAMELEON_*` variables.

## `chameleon_rs.configure()`

```python
import chameleon_rs

chameleon_rs.configure(
    template_folder='templates',
    auto_reload=False,
    restricted_namespace=True,
    strict_tags=True,
    strict_names=True,
    partial_search='caller',
    markdown=True,
    markdown_cache=1024,
)
```

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `template_folder` | none, required on the first call | An existing directory. Partials and the framework integrations load templates by name from it. |
| `auto_reload` | `False` | Recompile a template when its file changes. For partials, each file is checked at most once per render. Use it in development only. |
| `restricted_namespace` | `True` | `False` allows attributes with other namespaces or prefixes, such as Alpine.js's `@click` or Vue's `v-on:click`. |
| `strict_tags` | `False` (or `CHAMELEON_STRICT_TAGS`) | `True` makes an unclosed element carrying template attributes a `ParseError` that points at it. Recommended. See [Catching unclosed tags](strict-tags.qmd). |
| `strict_names` | `False` (or `CHAMELEON_STRICT_NAMES`) | `True` makes the decorator APIs (`@template`, `render`, `response`, `ErrorPage`'s template) refuse names that could leave the template folder, with the same `ValueError` as a missing template. For apps that build template names from request data. See [Security](security.qmd#template-names-from-requests). |
| `partial_search` | `'caller'` | Where `render_partial` looks: `'caller'` searches the template folder, then the calling template's search path and folders. `'registered'` searches the template folder only, as chameleon_partials does. See [Partials](partials.qmd#how-a-path-is-found). |
| `markdown` | none | The `markdown:` expression: `True` for the defaults, or a dict of profiles (prefix → options). `False` removes it. See [Markdown](markdown.qmd). |
| `markdown_cache` | `1024` | How many Markdown conversions to keep. `0` turns the cache off. |

How it behaves:

- **An option you leave out keeps its current value.** So
  `configure(partial_search='registered')` changes only the search mode.
- **Every call applies.** There's no `cache_init` as in chameleon_partials,
  chameleon-flask and fastapi-chameleon, so a second call with a different folder takes effect.
- **It's safe with threads.** Each configuration is an immutable object that's swapped in whole,
  so a render running at the same time never sees half of one. Still, call it at startup,
  not per request.
- **`partial_search` and the Markdown settings don't need a folder.** Every other option
  needs one, on the first call.
- It returns the new settings, and raises `chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError` for a missing
  folder, or `ValueError` for an unknown `partial_search` or an invalid Markdown setting
  (`TypeError` for one of the wrong type). A call that raises changes nothing.

```{python}
#| echo: false
import tempfile
template_folder = tempfile.mkdtemp()
```

```{python}
import chameleon_rs

settings = chameleon_rs.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=True)
print(settings.auto_reload, settings.restricted_namespace)

# Leaving options out keeps them: auto_reload is still True.
settings = chameleon_rs.configure(partial_search='registered')
print(settings.auto_reload)
```

For tests, `chameleon_rs.partials.clear()`, `chameleon_rs.flask.clear()`,
`chameleon_rs.fastapi.clear()`, `chameleon_rs.starlette.clear()`, `chameleon_rs.robyn.clear()` and
`chameleon_rs.litestar.clear()` forget the configuration again. Starlette's `Templates()` and
Litestar's `ChameleonEngine()` without a directory use this configuration too.

`chameleon_rs.flask.configure(..., app=app)` sets a configuration for one Flask or Quart app
only. See [Flask and Quart](flask.qmd#one-configuration-per-app).

## Template options

The template classes take Chameleon's options as keyword arguments, or as class attributes on
a subclass. `PageTemplateLoader` passes any extra keyword arguments on to each template it
loads.

```python
from chameleon_rs import PageTemplateFile, PageTemplateLoader

page = PageTemplateFile('templates/home.pt', auto_reload=True, encoding='utf-8')
templates = PageTemplateLoader(['templates'], '.pt', restricted_namespace=False)
```

The common ones:

| Option | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `auto_reload` | `False` (or `CHAMELEON_RELOAD`) | File templates recompile when their file changes. |
| `encoding` | none | Lets you pass encoded byte strings as values. |
| `translate` | none | The translation function for `i18n:` attributes: `translate(msgid, domain=None, mapping=None, default=None, context=None, target_language=None)`. |
| `boolean_attributes` | the HTML set, in HTML mode | Attributes rendered as `name="name"` for a true value and dropped for a false one. The default is Chameleon's XHTML 1.0 list; `chameleon_rs.template.HTML5_BOOLEAN_ATTRIBUTES` adds HTML5's (`required`, `autofocus`, ...). |
| `strict` | `True` | Compile every expression up front. `False` only requires an expression to be valid when it's evaluated. |
| `restricted_namespace` | `True` | `False` passes unknown namespaces and prefixes through, for Alpine.js or Vue. |
| `strict_tags` | `False` (or `CHAMELEON_STRICT_TAGS`) | chameleon-rs only. An unclosed element carrying `tal:`, `metal:` or `i18n:` attributes is a `ParseError` at its start tag, instead of an error far away or none at all. See [Catching unclosed tags](strict-tags.qmd). |
| `trim_attribute_space` | `False` | Strip extra whitespace between attributes. |
| `implicit_i18n_translate` | `False` | Mark the text in every element for translation. |
| `implicit_i18n_attributes` | empty | Attribute names (lowercase) to mark for translation. |
| `on_error_handler` | none | Called with the exception in a `tal:on-error` fallback. |
| `default_expression` | `'python'` | The expression type used when there's no prefix. |
| `extra_builtins` | empty | Extra names available in every template. |
| `keep_body` / `keep_source` | `False` | Keep the template's source text, or a readable dump of its compiled program. |

The rest are also accepted, as in Chameleon: `default_marker`, `value_repr`, `tokenizer`,
`debug`, `enable_data_attributes`, `enable_comment_interpolation` and `expression_types`.
File templates also take `search_path`, `package_name`, `loader_class` and
`prepend_relative_search_path`.

Paths can be `pathlib.Path` objects (any `os.PathLike`) anywhere a path string works: the
template's filename, a single search path or a list of them, and the name you look up in a
loader. Chameleon accepts only strings here
([malthe/chameleon#342](https://github.com/malthe/chameleon/issues/342)).

```python
from pathlib import Path

templates = PageTemplateLoader(Path(__file__).parent / 'templates', '.pt')
```

::: {.callout-note}
## `source` is a program dump, not Python

Chameleon compiles a template to a Python module, and `template.source` is that module's
code. chameleon-rs compiles to a native program instead, so with `keep_source=True`,
`source` holds a readable dump of the program. Nothing in Chameleon's own tests depends on
it being Python.
:::

## Environment variables

These are read once, when chameleon-rs is imported, as Chameleon reads them. The values `y`,
`yes`, `t`, `true`, `on` and `1` (any case) count as true.

| Variable | Effect |
|---|---|
| `CHAMELEON_RELOAD` | The default for `auto_reload`: file templates reload when their file changes. |
| `CHAMELEON_EAGER` | File templates compile when they're created, not on first use. Handy in a test that checks every template in a project compiles. |
| `CHAMELEON_DEBUG` | Templates keep their body and a dump of their compiled program, and use a module loader in a temporary directory. |
| `CHAMELEON_STRICT_TAGS` | chameleon-rs only. The default for `strict_tags`, for `configure()` and every template: unclosed elements carrying template attributes are errors. See [Catching unclosed tags](strict-tags.qmd). |
| `CHAMELEON_STRICT_NAMES` | chameleon-rs only. The default for `strict_names`: the decorator APIs refuse template names that could leave the template folder. See [Security](security.qmd#template-names-from-requests). |
| `CHAMELEON_CACHE` | A directory, which must exist. Chameleon writes the generated Python modules there. chameleon-rs checks the directory but doesn't write compiled programs to disk: compiling is fast enough not to need it. |

Unknown `CHAMELEON_*` variables are logged as warnings, as in Chameleon.



## Web frameworks

### Web frameworks

chameleon-rs works with the Python web frameworks you're likely to use, with nothing extra to
install. Each integration is a module of chameleon-rs that imports its framework only when you
import it, and uses the version your app already has.

| Framework | Use | It replaces | Guide |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flask, Quart | `chameleon_rs.flask` | chameleon-flask | [Flask and Quart](flask.qmd) |
| FastAPI | `chameleon_rs.fastapi` | fastapi-chameleon | [FastAPI](fastapi.qmd) |
| Starlette | `chameleon_rs.starlette` | Starlette's `Jinja2Templates` | [Starlette](starlette.qmd) |
| Robyn | `chameleon_rs.robyn` | chameleon-robyn | [Robyn](robyn.qmd) |
| Litestar | `chameleon_rs.litestar` | Litestar's Jinja engine, litestar-chameleon | [Litestar](litestar.qmd) |
| Pyramid | pyramid_chameleon, unchanged | (runs through `compat.install()`) | [Pyramid](pyramid.qmd) |

Already using one of the libraries in the third column? `chameleon_rs.compat.install()` makes
its import give the built-in, so the app runs unchanged. See
[Switching from Chameleon](switching-from-chameleon.qmd).

## The same page in each framework

Each example renders `templates/home/index.pt`:

```html
<h1>${title}</h1>
<ul><li tal:repeat="v videos">${v}</li></ul>
```

::: {.panel-tabset}

## Flask

```python
import flask

import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder='templates', app=app)


@app.get('/')
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')
def index():
    return {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': ['intro', 'partials']}
```

## Quart

```python
import quart

import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask

app = quart.Quart(__name__)
chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder='templates', app=app)


@app.get('/')
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')
async def index():
    return {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': await load_videos()}
```

## FastAPI

```python
import fastapi

import chameleon_rs.fastapi as fastapi_chameleon

app = fastapi.FastAPI()
fastapi_chameleon.configure(template_folder='templates', app=app)


@app.get('/')
@fastapi_chameleon.template('home/index.pt')
async def index():
    return {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': await load_videos()}
```

## Starlette

```python
from starlette.applications import Starlette
from starlette.routing import Route

from chameleon_rs.starlette import Templates

templates = Templates(directory='templates')


async def index(request):
    model = {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': await load_videos()}
    return await templates.TemplateResponse_async(request, 'home/index.pt', model)


app = Starlette(routes=[Route('/', index)])
```

## Robyn

```python
from robyn import Robyn

import chameleon_rs.robyn as chameleon_robyn

app = Robyn(__file__)
chameleon_robyn.configure(template_folder='templates', app=app)


@app.get('/')
@chameleon_robyn.template('home/index.pt')
async def index():
    return {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': await load_videos()}
```

## Litestar

```python
from litestar import Litestar, get

import chameleon_rs.litestar as chameleon_litestar


@get('/')
@chameleon_litestar.template('home/index.pt')
async def index() -> dict:
    return {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': await load_videos()}


app = Litestar([index])
chameleon_litestar.configure(template_folder='templates', app=app)
```

## Pyramid

```python
import chameleon_rs.compat

chameleon_rs.compat.install()   # first, before pyramid_chameleon is imported

from pyramid.config import Configurator
from pyramid.view import view_config


@view_config(route_name='home', renderer='templates/home/index.pt')
def index(request):
    return {'title': 'Latest videos', 'videos': ['intro', 'partials']}


def main(global_config, **settings):
    with Configurator(settings=settings) as config:
        config.include('pyramid_chameleon')
        config.add_route('home', '/')
        config.scan()
    return config.make_wsgi_app()
```

:::

## What the integrations share

Flask, FastAPI, Starlette, Robyn and Litestar have the same decorator API, so what you learn
on one carries over:

- **`configure(template_folder=..., auto_reload=..., app=app)`** is the same call as
  `chameleon_rs.configure()`: one setup for views, partials and Markdown. Every call applies.
  `global_init(...)` is the original libraries' name and still works.
- **`@template('page.pt')`** renders what the view returns: a `dict`, any mapping, a dataclass
  or a Pydantic model. A framework response passes through unchanged, for redirects.
  `status_code=` and `content_type=` set the response; bare `@template` picks
  `{module}/{function}.html` or `.pt`.
- **`not_found()` and `error(template_file, status_code=500)`** end a view with an error page.
- **`render()` and `response()`**, with `render_async()` and `response_async()`, render
  without the decorator: an email body, a feed, an HTMX fragment.
- **`check_views(app)`** and **`clear()`** for tests.
- **Errors** share one base class, `chameleon_rs.web.TemplateError`, whichever module raised
  them.

### Async views

An `async def` view renders with `render_async`: a model value that is awaitable is awaited
where the template uses it, and the render doesn't block the event loop while it waits. A
plain `def` view renders with `render()`, where the framework runs it. See
[Async rendering](async.qmd) for the details and the opt-in concurrency settings.

### What a template gets

| Integration | Besides the model |
|---|---|
| Flask, Quart, FastAPI, Robyn | Nothing: the template gets what the view returns, as with the original libraries. Return `request` in the model if the template needs it. |
| Starlette | `request` and `url_for`, as with `Jinja2Templates`, plus its context processors with `Templates`. |
| Litestar | `request`, `csrf_input`, `url_for`, `csrf_token`, `url_for_static_asset` and your registered template callables. |
| Pyramid | `request`, `context`, `view` and `renderer_name`. |

Every template also has `render_partial` built in, and `markdown:` once it's turned on.

### Decorator order

`@template` goes below the route decorator:

```python
@app.get('/')                         # first: the route...
@chameleon_flask.template('page.pt')  # ...then @template
def index(): ...
```

Written the other way round, the router registers the bare view, the template never renders
and the route quietly returns the view's dict as JSON. Pass `app=` to `configure()` and the
mistake fails loudly with a `DecoratorOrderError` that names the view and the fix: when the app
starts (FastAPI, Starlette, Quart, Robyn, Litestar) or on the first request (Flask, which has
no startup hook). Each guide has the details.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Template names come from your code

The names given to `@template`, `render()`, `response()`, the error pages and
`render_partial()` are looked up as the original libraries look them up, which allows `..` and
absolute paths. Write them in your code; never build one from a request (a path or query
parameter, a header). Starlette's `Templates` and Litestar's `ChameleonEngine` refuse names
that reach outside their folder, as Jinja does.
:::


### Flask and Quart

`chameleon_rs.flask` renders templates from Flask and Quart views. It has chameleon-flask's
API, so moving an app over is an import change, or no change at all with
`chameleon_rs.compat.install()`.

`import chameleon_rs` doesn't import Flask. Only `import chameleon_rs.flask` does.

## A first view

```{python}
#| echo: false
import pathlib, tempfile

folder = pathlib.Path(tempfile.mkdtemp()) / 'templates'
for sub in ('home', 'errors', 'shared'):
    (folder / sub).mkdir(parents=True)
(folder / 'home' / 'index.pt').write_text(
    '<h1>${message}</h1>\n'
    '<ul><li tal:repeat="v videos">${render_partial(\'shared/video.pt\', video=v)}</li></ul>'
)
(folder / 'shared' / 'video.pt').write_text('<a href="/videos/${video}">${video}</a>')
(folder / 'errors' / '404.pt').write_text('<h1>Not found: ${path}</h1>')
template_folder = str(folder)
dev_mode = True
```

```{python}
import flask

import chameleon_rs.flask as chameleon_flask

app = flask.Flask(__name__)
chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder=template_folder, auto_reload=dev_mode)


@app.get('/')
@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')
def index():
    return {'message': 'Hello', 'videos': ['intro', 'partials']}
```

The view returns the template's model, and `@template` renders it into a `flask.Response`:

```{python}
client = app.test_client()
print(client.get('/').text)
```

`configure()` here is the same call as `chameleon_rs.configure()`, so it also tells
`render_partial` where templates live.

## Decorator order

`@template` goes below the route decorator. Written above it, Flask registers the bare view,
the template never renders and the route quietly returns the view's dict as JSON. Give the
app to `configure()` and it checks before its first request (Quart: when it starts serving):

```python
chameleon_flask.configure(template_folder=template_folder, app=app)


@chameleon_flask.template('home/index.pt')   # wrong: above the route
@app.get('/about')
def about():
    return {'message': 'About', 'videos': []}

# The first request raises chameleon_rs.web.DecoratorOrderError:
# @template must be placed below the route decorator (@app.route, @app.get,
# @blueprint.route, ...) on about() at app.py:12 (route GET /about): ...
```
